#pragma GCC optimize('O3,unroll-loops,fast-math') — function-level pragma applied to entire file (before class definition); fast-math can break floating-point comparisons elsewhere

#pragma unroll 4 before inline function definition (not before a loop) — GCC does NOT recognize #pragma unroll (it requires #pragma GCC unroll). Clang may recognize it. This pragma is in the wrong location (before function, not before a loop).
Same #pragma unroll 4 placement issue as line 27
get_bid(uint32_t level) has NO bounds check — if level >= MAX_LEVELS (100), returns reference to array element past end. Undefined Behavior in hot path. Same issue on line 45 for get_ask().
__attribute__((packed)) on Level2Entry — packing can cause unaligned memory access, potentially reducing performance on some architectures despite saving space

sequence_.load(std::memory_order_acquire) — correct for SPSC consumer, but sequence_ is only written in update_bid/update_ask which use relaxed; the acquire load provides no guarantee without a corresponding release store on the producer side for cross-thread visibility

T item = buffer_[current_tail]; — copies element out; then line 49: buffer_[current_tail].~T() — explicit destructor call. For non-trivially-destructible types, after the copy, the original is destroyed but the slot remains 'constructed' in memory. When the unique_ptr<T[]> destructor later calls ~T() on ALL slots, already-destructed slots get double-destroyed → UB. Safe ONLY for trivially destructible types like AlphaSignal (which is currently the case).

new (&buffer_[current_head]) T(item) — placement new copy-constructs into the slot. If T has a non-trivial copy constructor that allocates, this creates heap allocations in the hot path. AlphaSignal is POD so this is fine, but the template is not safe for general use.

buffer_ = std::make_unique<T[]>(Capacity) — allocates on heap at construction. Comment says 'buffer allocated once at init' — correctly zero-alloc after init, but the unique_ptr adds a pointer indirection

next_head == tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire) — full capacity is usable but with one slot wasted (next_head wraps before tail catches up). Capacity 4096 means 4095 usable slots. The benchmark pre-fills 4095 (correct), but documentation may be misleading about actual capacity.
static constexpr size_t mask_ = Capacity - 1 — requires Capacity to be power of 2 (asserted at line 17). This is correct but limits flexibility.

core/crypto/eip712_signer.hpp.description: EIP-712 signer with Keccak-256 implementation and OpenSSL ECDSA signing
core/crypto/eip712_signer.hpp.runtime_verification: keccak256_hash(empty_string) produces a6088b47e77469abeca03f18f4b6f563465e73236ebfe025df792869665135f0 — expected c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470. Keccak-256 IS BROKEN.

issues.description: keccak256_hash() function — while the implementation is a full Keccak-f[1600] permutation (NOT a SHA-256 stub as previously audited), it produces INCORRECT output. Verified at runtime: keccak256('') = a6088b47... instead of c5d24601... Root cause: the π (pi) step at line 100 has x/y coordinates swapped in the destination index. Line 100: 'int dest = y * 5 + (2 * x + 3 * y) % 5;' should be 'int dest = y + 5 * ((2 * x + 3 * y) % 5);' to correctly map B[y, (2x+3y)%5] instead of B[(2x+3y)%5, y].

memcpy(padded, data, len) — no bounds check; if len > RSIZ (136 bytes), buffer overflow on stack. Keccak-256 should handle multi-block messages (absorb in 136-byte chunks), but this only processes a single block.
padded[len] = 0x01 — if len == RSIZ (136), this writes past the stack buffer (out-of-bounds). The padding logic does not handle the edge case where the message fills the entire block.

static const std::array<uint8_t, 32> domain_sep = {{0xAB}} — domain separator is a placeholder (0xAB followed by 31 zero bytes), NOT the actual EIP-712 domain separator. The correct domain separator must be keccak256('EIP712Domain' + typehash + salt + verifier + chain_id + ...). Without the real domain separator, signatures are not bound to Polymarket's domain — replay cross-domain.

EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_signature_md(sign_ctx, EVP_sha256()) + EVP_PKEY_sign(sign_ctx, ..., eip712_hash, 32) — DOUBLE HASHING BUG. OpenSSL will SHA-256 the already-hashed eip712_hash (32 bytes) before signing. EIP-712 requires signing the raw Keccak-256 digest directly. Should use EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_signature_md(sign_ctx, nullptr) for raw digest signing, or use ECDSA_sign() direct.

out_signature[64] = 27 — recovery id (v) hardcoded to 27. Ethereum secp256k1 ECDSA requires v to be 27 or 28 based on the y-parity of the public key point used in the nonce. Hardcoding 27 means ~50% of signatures will have incorrect v and be unrecoverable by Polymarket's on-chain verification.

const BIGNUM* priv_bn = BN_bin2bn(...) — missing BN_free check and the BIGNUM is freed at line 172 but if EC_KEY_set_private_key fails at line 153, the error handler throws without freeing priv_bn or pub_key (memory leak on error path)

EC_KEY* ec_key = EVP_PKEY_get1_EC_KEY(pkey_) — this increments the reference count on ec_key. Then line 168: EVP_PKEY_set1_EC_KEY(pkey_, ec_key) increments it again. Line 174: EC_KEY_free(ec_key) decrements once. The net reference count may not be 1, potentially leaking or prematurely freeing.

EVP_PKEY_keygen generates a RANDOM key pair, then the code overwrites the private key with the provided one. The generated public key is computed from the random private key, then overwritten. This is wasteful (generates + discards a random keypair) and the order of operations (generate then overwrite) could fail if OpenSSL 3.x validates the key internally.
std::vector<uint8_t> der_signature(sig_len) — heap allocation in sign_order (hot path). EIP-712 signing should be zero-allocation.
std::vector<uint8_t> struct_data(sizeof(OrderParams)) — another heap allocation in sign_order hot path for a struct that is already a fixed-size POD

#pragma GCC optimize('-O3') — function-level optimization pragma pushes optimization but the comment on line 14 claims 'full Keccak-256 implementation (FIPS 202 compliant)' — it is technically NIST SHA-3/Keccak-f[1600] but with the π bug it is NOT FIPS 202 compliant

missing_dependencies: Real EIP-712 domain separator computation (hash of EIP712Domain type definition)
Proper ECDSA recovery id (v) calculation from y-parity
Raw digest signing path (no double SHA-256 hashing)
Per-message random salt generation (crypto-grade RNG)
OpenSSL <openssl/ecdsa.h> explicitly included (uses ECDSA_SIG implicitly via d2i_ECDSA_SIG and ECDSA_SIG_get0)

issues.description: calculate_fractional_kelly(ev, confidence, fraction=0.1) — oversimplified Kelly: optimal_f = ev * confidence. The actual Kelly criterion for binary outcomes is f* = (bp - q)/b where b=odds, p=win_prob, q=1-p. The approximation ev*confidence is NOT mathematically equivalent and can produce incorrect position sizes.
No risk-free rate, no drawdown consideration, no position cap relative to available capital — simplified for demo

tests/benchmarks/latency_bench.cpp.description: Latency benchmark using RDTSC to measure hot path cycles

issues.description: Benchmark measures engine.run_tick() which calls EIP712Signer::sign_order() — this invokes OpenSSL ECDSA_sign() which is a HEAVY operation (crypto on CPU). The 288µs minimum is dominated by OpenSSL crypto, NOT the hot path logic. The documented '24 cycles / 7.8ns' in docs/OPTIMIZATION_LINEAGE.md is INVALID — the real measurement is ~289µs.

Pre-fills QUEUE_CAPACITY-1 (4095) signals, but refills at lines 55 and 86 attempt to push 4095 items into a queue that may already have items. try_push returns false when full, but the refill logic doesn't check or compensate — many refills silently fail.
CPU frequency calibration uses sleep(100ms) between rdtscp calls — sleep is interrupted by OS scheduler, introducing jitter. More precise calibration uses RDTSC vs clock_gettime in a tight loop.

printf with '%.3f us' uses ns_per_cycle * cycles / 1000.0 — the calibration divides chrono ns by cycle delta. The runtime showed 0.372 ns/cycle — this implies a 2.7 GHz CPU which is plausible, but the latency (288µs min) is entirely from OpenSSL crypto, making the 'hot path' measurement meaningless.

int main() { run_latency_test(); return 0; } — no CTest registration, no pass/fail assertion. CI workflow runs './bin/crowdintel_bot' instead (see CI workflow line 33), which is the demo, not the benchmark.

Includes bench_engine.hpp which has #include 'eip712_signer.hpp' — the benchmark measures crypto signing latency, not pure hot path latency. A proper hot-path-only benchmark would use MockCLOBClient and skip signing.
